Surgical Breast Enlargement

Recovery After Breast Reduction

Recovery varies with technique and extent. Your surgeon’s advice comes first, especially in the first weeks.

Home/Surgical Breast Enlargement/Breast reduction/Recovery After Breast Reduction

Recovery varies with technique and extent. Your surgeon’s advice comes first, especially in the first weeks.

The first days

  • Soreness, swelling, bruising and tightness
  • Dressings and a surgical bra
  • Possible drains
  • Altered sensation in the breasts and nipples
  • Tiredness

Some people feel immediate relief from weight and strain even while sore.

Medicines

You will usually have pain relief. Follow instructions on which medicines to avoid, since some raise bleeding risk.

Activity

  • Walk gently from early on
  • Avoid lifting, pushing and strenuous exercise for several weeks
  • Avoid reaching overhead and sudden movements if advised
  • Return to office-type work after a period set by your surgeon, and to physical work later

Sleeping and support

Sleeping on your back with your upper body raised is often advised. Wear the recommended bra as instructed, day and night at first.

Wounds and scars

Keep dressings clean and dry, and attend wound checks. Scars begin red and raised and fade over a year or more. Protect them from the sun.

Healing at scar junctions

The point where scars meet can heal slowly in some people, sometimes needing dressings for a while.

Shape

Breasts look swollen and high at first, and settle over weeks to months.

Work, caregiving and lifting

Plan ahead for meals, transport, childcare and tasks that need pushing, pulling or carrying. Even if desk work feels possible early, fatigue and limited arm movement can make a full day difficult. Ask for separate guidance on returning to office work, manual work, driving and exercise.

Follow-up and gradual activity

Attend planned wound checks and ask when it is safe to change bras, sleep on your side, raise your arms freely and restart each type of exercise. Returning too quickly can stress healing wounds. Your plan may change if there is delayed healing, a seroma or a scar problem.

Longer-term changes

Numbness, scar colour and breast shape can continue to change for many months. Keep routine breast care and tell imaging teams about the operation. A new lump, discharge or persistent one-sided change still needs medical assessment.

Call your surgeon if

You have fever, spreading redness, discharge, rapid swelling on one side, a wound opening, or a nipple turning dark, pale or cold. See warning signs.

Key takeaway

Plan for rest and help at home. See Breast Reduction.
